title: Brand statement from prison claiming his innocence ‘appalling’ and could breach rules, says No 10 – UK politics live
description:
Brand’s wife Laura read out a message from him on their YouTube show

After education questions, there is one urgent question in the Commons and two ministerial statements. They are, with rough timings:

3.30pm: A Home Office minister responds to an urgent question about planning permission being granted for the proposed camp for asylum seekers near Piddington.

It’s always a good idea to promote closer cooperation with all of our allies, and there’s always more that you can do to facilitate trade with friends and neighbours. However, what I disagree with is a settlement that will involve us paying hundreds of millions of pounds into the EU and involve the imposition of huge amounts of red tape on all sorts of businesses across the country … I think it’s a really bad step backwards.
text: Early evening summary

The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences just days after his conviction.
Barristers could be barred from practice if they perpetuate rape myths to defend clients, Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has said after Russell Brand’s trial.
Andy Burnham will in a speech tonight set out three tests for his EU reset so that it brings Brexit “closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016”, No 10 has said. (See 10.59am.)

James Frith, a health minister, has told MPs that the Department of Health and Social Care is not going to stop the US firm Palantir running a key NHS data contract – but that it is launching a procurement process that could lead to other suppliers taking over in future. (See 5.41pm.) In the Commons, the Labour leftwinger John McDonnell said the new contract should include a requirement for a provider to have a “humanitarian track record” so Palantir can be told “no need to apply”.

An outage affecting Microsoft products is not thought to have put NHS patients’ safety at risk, a minister has said. As the Press Association reports, online safety minister Ian Murray said while most health services remained up and running during a global outage last week, “this incident could have been more serious if it lasted longer”. Microsoft services were disrupted throughout Friday, with millions of the technology giant’s customers unable to send and receive emails through Outlook. Teams, Copilot AI assistant and other Microsoft 365 services were also disrupted. On Saturday morning, a statement from the US-based firm confirmed the “underlying issue of the incident” had been addressed with services restored. Making a statement in Parliament, Murray told the Commons “there is no indication the incident was caused by malicious activity”.
For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.
Palantir gets NHS data contract extended, as minister says new process could be 'bridge' to British firms taking over in future

James Frith, a health minister, has told MPs that the Department of Health and Social Care is not going to stop the US firm Palantir running a key NHS data contract – but that it is launching a procurement process that could lead to other suppliers taking over in future.
In a statement to MPs, he said government priorities had moved on since Palantir won the contract to run the NHS’s federated data platform (FDP).
Palantir’s involvement has been hugely controversial because of the work it does for Donald Trump’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and for the Israeli military.
Some MPs wanted the government to use a break clause in the Palantir contract to get the firm out of the NHS now.

Frith confirmed that is not happening. The Palantir contract will run until March 2029. But Frith said that a new procurement process is being launched, and he described that as a “bridge” to an alternative arrangement.

double quotation markToday I can update the house that we will begin a new procurement process along different lines from the current contract. From January, the NHS will begin this vital work with patients, our partners and the market. Formal procurement will begin in the second half of next year and we expect the full process from engagement to completion to take around 18 months.
This was about “opening the next generation of FDP” to other suppliers, he said.

double quotation markInnovative providers will be invited to help address the data and digital fragmentation in this important area of care, and test how health priorities can create routes to build UK AI capability.
In response, Chi Onwurah, the Labour chair of the science committee, said this was a missed opportunity. She said:

double quotation markMy committee has repeatedly called on the government to exercise the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s federated data platform contract with the NHS. It’s deeply disappointing to hear that it won’t do so and is instead choosing to extend the contract for two years, during which time it says it will procure a UK-based supplier. The suggestion that exercising the break clause now would be too impractical only reinforces our concerns about vendor lock-in - procurement decisions have left the NHS dependent on a single supplier without a straightforward route out … Palantir is not the only company capable of providing this kind of middleware technology. Our critical public services shouldn’t be so heavily dependent on a single US-based supplier for their digital infrastructure - last Friday’s Outlook outage was a stark reminder of why resilience and technological sovereignty matter.
Minister accuses Tories of hypocrisy over Piddington, and of ignoring evidence implying migrant camps don't increase crime

Anna Turley, a Home Office minister, has accused the Conservatives of hypocrisy after they revived claims that placing a camp for more than 1,000 asylum seekers near Piddington, a small village in Oxfordshire, will lead to a rise in crime.

Turley pointed out that when the Tories were in power they also opened camps for asylum seekers in former military bases, and she accused them of ignoring evidence that this did not create a crime problem.
She was speaking in the Commons in response to an urgent question about the decision, announced last week, to grant planning permission for the proposed camp at Piddington.

Turley told MPs that the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government approved the planning application and that it was subject to conditions. She said the Home Office was still assessing the feasibility of using MoD Bicester for asylum accommodation, and that a final decision had not been taken.

The residents of Piddington have fought a high-profile campaign to block the plan, including holding a notional referendum on independence. The Conservatives and Reform UK have strongly supported them, and to a large extent the campaign has focused on the supposed risk that the mostly-male asylum seekers in the camp might pose to women and girls in the village.

In her opening response to the UQ, Turley said that the people of Piddington had expressed their views powerfully and that she respected them for it. But she also said the government had a duty to act in the national interest and she defended housing asylum seekers in military camps as an alternative to the “costly and wholly unsustainable use of hotels”.

Joy Morrissey, the shadow minister for women and equalities, said the government “chose to put women and girls in Piddington at risk – risk they knew would come from the horrific crimes committed by other illegal migrant men against girls as young as 12” when it approved the planning application.
double quotation markWhy is the government approving the site in full knowledge that they cannot ensure the safety of women and girls? This is a decision that the government will come to regret.
In response, Turley asked if Morrissey had come to regret the decision taken by the Tories when they were in office to house asylum seekers at Wethersfield, a former RAF base in Essex. She went on:

double quotation mark[Morrissey] raised the concerns about local crime rates, but I wonder if she’s actually been there to listen to the fact that at Wethersfield, which has been operating for a number of years, there has been no evidence of rising crime in the area. In fact, the chief constable of Essex police stated on the 11 September that crime linked to the Wethersfield site is very low and that there is no reason for the public to be concerned about possible criminality in the area associated with the site. In fact, Braintree is one of the lowest crime areas in the country and sees fewer incidents now compared to when the site was opened three years ago.
Turley also said that the “brass neck” Morrissey was displaying was “astonishing” given that the last government “lost control” of the asylum system.

Some asylum seekers do commit violent crimes, and there is evidence that some national groups prominent in the asylum-seeking community are proportionately more likely to engage in sexual offending than other people in Britain. But the extent of the threat has been vastly exaggerated by anti-migrant rightwingers. Emma Monk posted a good guide to what the actual data reveals on her Monk Debunks Substack blog last week.

The Commons liaison committee, which regularly holds an evidence session with the prime minister, normally three times a year, has announced that it will question Andy Burnham for the first time two weeks today, on Monday 30 November. The session will focus on “the UK’s resilience in the face of global and domestic challenges”, the committee says.
David Chadwick has been confirmed as the new leader of the Liberal Democrats in Wales.
As the BBC reports, the Lib Dems have only one MP in Wales – Chadwick, who is MP for Brecon, Radnor and Cwm Tawe – and one member of the Senedd, Jane Dodds.
With Dodds standing down as the Welsh Lib Dem leader, Chadwick was the only person eligible to replace her.

double quotation markAt a time when politics is increasingly dominated by division and populism, I believe the Liberal Democrats have something different to offer. A politics that believes in people, gives them the tools to succeed and is prepared to take difficult decisions to improve their lives.
Government will need legislation to implement UK-EU reset on food standards, Falconer tells MPs
Lisa O’Carroll is a senior Guardian correspondent covering post-Brexit affairs.
Primary legislation will be required to bring the UK in line with EU laws on food and drink standards, Hamish Falconer, the EU relations minister, has told MPs.

Falconer told MPs and MEPs at a meeting of the UK-EU parliamentary partnership assembly that measures being announced on Friday as part of a reset deal would have to be implemented via legislation. (See 2.29pm.)
Legislation is particularly required for the measures relating to farming and disease.
This is why implementation of the deal, which was originally envisaged to be in the summer of 2027, is likely to be delayed until the first quarter of 2028, sources say.
Badenoch says her personal view is that age of consent should go up to 18

At her press conference this morning, Kemi Badenoch suggested she was not in favour of having a staggered age of consent because she did not think that would be practical. (See 10.30am.) As Dominic Penna reports at the Telegraph, in an interview on ITV’s Good Morning Britain this morning she said that personally she would like to see the age of consent go up to 18. But that was not party policy, she stressed.

double quotation markIf it was up to me personally – this is not Conservative party policy – I would just make the age of majority 18 for everything. There’s too much randomness in the system. Let childhood be childhood, everything at 18.
EU minister Hamish Falconer says he's 'optimistic' UK car industry will get opt-out from EU's Made in Europe restrictions

The Labour MP Nia Griffith asked if the UK automobile sector was likely to included in the Made in Europe programme (a new protectionist scheme banning items from being included in public procurement contracts if they are not mostly made in the EU).
Falconer said this was still being negotiated, but he said he was “pretty optimistic” of a good outcome for Britain. He explained:

double quotation markI think it is absolutely obvious that the European car industry, whether in the UK or the EU, is facing real competitive pressures. My strong view is that the best way to respond to those pressures is not to make the European car industry smaller and more expensive, which would be the function of segmenting the supply chains in any meaningful way. We of course, discussed that with our friends in the European Union. There is, as you know, a busy debate within the EU about what approach should be taken on these issues, whether in relation to the Industrial Accelerator Act or in other areas. I think the case for the UK being a close, trusted partner to the EU in these industrial issues is so strong that I’m pretty optimistic that we will come to a sensible conclusion. I can’t, of course, speak for the EU or indeed forestall their legislative process. This is an ongoing EU debate. But I’m – for myself, speaking only personally – relatively optimistic that I think this will arrive in a sensible place.
Šefčovič said he agreed with the gist of this. He said it was “in the interest of both of us” to work on “the resilience of our automotive supply chains”.
The Labour MP Stella Creasy, chair of the Labour Movement for Europe, asked if the UK could learn from Switzerland’s relationship with the EU.
Falconer did not reply in detail, but he said the government was “really ambitious for a, deeper, closer, stronger relationship with the European Union”.
Explaining the EU’s relationship with Switzerland, Šefčovič said:

double quotation markThe model we have in Switzerland is comprehensive. It means that it engages with the EU on most aspects of the internal market. And, in exchange for this access, Switzerland contributes financially to our cohesion policy, with many cohesion projects supported directly with the Swiss funds. So Switzerland also accepts free movement of persons and participates in the Schengen area. Where Switzerland does participate in the internal internal market, agreements rely on dynamic alignments and the uniform interpretation and application of the EU law which ensures, in turn, the level playing field for all participants in the internal market.
Šefčovič said it was up to the UK to decide what relationship with the EU it wanted.
Burnham wants 'big, broad discussion' about future relationship with EU, minister says
Falconer and Šefčovič are now taking questions.
In response to a question from Mika Aaltola, a Finnish MEP, about whether Andy Burnham’s EU reset could lead to the UK rejoining at some point, Falconer replied:

double quotation markThe question you’re asking me is really, are we prepared to have a big, broad discussion in the UK about the future relationship between the UK and the European Union? And the answer is yes. I won’t get ahead of the prime minister who’s going to give a speech this evening when he’ll say a little bit about this. What he will often say to me is you cannot think about the UK’s path ahead over the next 10 years without thinking about our relationship with our home continent, and that is very much the spirit in which he comes to this. So I think you’ll hear more from us soon. And he is prepared to have a broad discussion about that.
EU trade commissioner confirms UK will have to pay for access to EU's internal electricity market

Maroš Šefčovič, who as the European commissioner for trade is the EU’s lead negotiator with the UK on post-Brexit issues, told the UK-EU parliamentary partnership assembly that he hoped agreements would be reached on Friday in relation to three areas: sanitary and phytosanitary standards, emissions trading and youth experience.

He said the UK and the EU would also continue negotiating on UK participation in the EU’s internal electricity market. This would involve the UK making a contribution to the EU’s cohesion funds because this was a condition of particpation in the internal market, he said. He said these agreements would not be ready this week.
He said the youth experience scheme was particularly important because “young people are always the best ambassadors of our countries”.

double quotation markWe also want to build a closer, more resilient partnership between the EU and United Kingdom. And this partnership will put cooperation on economic security at its heart. That is why the summit will discuss how to cooperate more closely whether we can protect joint supply chains and under what conditions.
Reset deals coming on Friday should be 'floor, not ceiling' of government's ambition for closer UK-EU relations, minister says
Hamish Falconer told the UK-EU parliamentary partnership assembly that the TCA (trade and cooperation agreement – the post-Brexit trade deal with the EU) has now been in force for five years.
The rest would provide an opportunity to” cut costs, support industries and create more opportunities for young people”, he said.

double quotation markAt the heart of what our teams have been doing are the detailed negotiations on the three new agreements we committed to last year – an agrifood trade deal, an agreement to link our emissions trading systems and a youth experience scheme. These important deals will boost our respective economies. They will cut red tape, help our businesses grow and provide opportunities to young people denied since Brexit. Over the course of this week, Maroš [Šefčovič] and I will be working hard to conclude those agreements and we hope to have good news for you come Friday summit. The UK government will then bring forward primary legislation to implement those agreements. We will also discuss a shared approach to protecting our economic security to ensure we do not unintentionally harm each other, and instead tackle shared economic challenges together. That should be the floor, not the ceiling, of our ambition. We want to go further to restore a higher level of growth and prosperity. So beyond this summit, as the prime minister said, we will begin to look at options for the future and opening a national discussion on these options. And that is obviously also a conversation we will want to have with our EU partners and friends about how Britain and the EU can work more closely together for our common security, prosperity and opportunity.

Hamish Falconer, the minister for EU relations, and his EU counterpart, Maroš Šefčovič, are both speaking and taking questions at a meeting of the UK-EU parliamentary partnership assembly in the House of Commons today. There is a live feed here. Falconer and Šefčovič have been heavily involved in the EU deals being announced on Friday, although it is not clear how much they will want to reveal this afternoon. Falconer started by saying he was appointed to his job while he was on honeymoon. He said he would not describe himself as married to Šefčovič, but they spend so much time together “it sometimes feels like the relationship is indeed very close,” he joked.
No 10 declines to rule out UK taking part in EU Rwanda scheme for failed asylum seekers
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the European Union’s pilot scheme to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, the Press Association reports. PA says:

double quotation markSeveral EU countries are reportedly set to announce a deal to send rejected asylum seekers to the east African country. The government will watch the scheme “with interest” as part of efforts to find “innovative approaches” to kerb illegal migration, No 10 said. The scandal-hit Rwanda deportation plan introduced under the Conservatives was axed by Keir Starmer immediately after he became prime minister. It cost Britain £700m despite only four volunteers being sent to Kigali, then-home secretary Yvette Cooper said, as she branded the policy the “most shocking waste of taxpayer money I have ever seen”. But the new EU pilot is said to differ from the Tory plan because it will only apply to asylum seekers who have exhausted all of their options, rather than all asylum seekers who arrive. Asked about the scheme, the PM’s spokesperson said: “I’ve seen the reports on this. Obviously, it’s for the EU to make any announcements. I’m not going to get ahead of that. “More broadly, though, you’ve got our position. The UK, like other European countries, is exploring innovative approaches to tackle illegal migration, including returns hubs, and will continue working with international partners to strengthen returns, remove those with no right to be here and restore control to our borders.” Asked to rule out the UK joining the plan, the spokesperson said the UK would be watching the new initiative “with interest, learning from what went on in the past”.
